name: Reinke oedema
aliases: polypoid degeneration of the vocal folds

clinicalPearls: Diffuse gelatinous swelling of the superficial lamina propria (Reinke's space) producing bilateral, floppy, oedematous vocal folds
Strongly associated with cigarette smoking, often compounded by vocal abuse and laryngopharyngeal reflux
Classically causes a characteristically deep, gravelly, low-pitched voice, particularly noticeable and distressing in women
Usually bilateral though frequently asymmetrical, with the mucosa billowing on inspiration
Smoking cessation is the single most important intervention and can halt progression
Bulky disease is treated by microlaryngeal surgery to evacuate the gelatinous material and redrape the mucosa, staged for each side to avoid webbing
Sudden change or a firm focal area in a heavy smoker should prompt exclusion of coexisting dysplasia or carcinoma
reference.pathophysiology: Reinke oedema is a chronic accumulation of oedematous, myxoid material within the superficial lamina propria of the vocal fold, the potential space known as Reinke's space. Prolonged irritation, above all from tobacco smoke, together with phonotrauma and reflux, increases vascular permeability and impairs lymphatic drainage in this loosely bound layer, so fluid and mucoid matrix collect and the covering mucosa becomes lax and redundant. The increased mass lowers the fundamental frequency of vibration, producing the typical low, rough voice, and in advanced disease the pendulous folds can narrow the airway.
additionalInvestigations: Flexible fibreoptic laryngoscopy to confirm diffuse bilateral polypoid change
Videostroboscopy to assess the mucosal wave and exclude a focal lesion
Thyroid function assessment where myxoedema is suspected
Histology of excised mucosa to exclude dysplasia or malignancy in smokers
redFlags: A firm or leukoplakic focal area suggesting dysplasia or carcinoma
Stridor or exertional dyspnoea from bulky airway-narrowing folds
Rapid unilateral change out of keeping with symmetrical polypoid degeneration
reference.prognosis: Progression usually halts with smoking cessation, and surgery reliably reduces bulk and raises vocal pitch, though the deepened voice may not fully normalise; continued smoking leads to recurrence and carries ongoing malignant risk.
pitfalls: Operating on both vocal folds simultaneously with aggressive mucosal removal, risking an anterior glottic web
Failing to insist on smoking cessation, allowing recurrence
Overlooking coexisting carcinoma masked by diffuse polypoid change
Attributing the low voice solely to habit and missing treatable hypothyroidism
references: Cummings Otolaryngology: Head and Neck Surgery
Scott-Brown's Otorhinolaryngology, Head and Neck Surgery
